A small kitchen at 6 a.m. on a January morning has a particular quality. The light comes in thin and pale through the window above the sink, making the room feel smaller, more honest. A window screen, fogged with condensation, holds a tiny cloud of breath-shaped patterns that dissolve every few seconds.

The kettle is on. You hear it before you feel its heat — this low, eager hum. A spoon rests in a wooden bowl holding oatmeal cooled into a faintly rubbery skin. Outside, a crow moves along the gutter with the deliberate, slightly offended walk of a landlord inspecting property.

There is a silence in the kitchen that isn't really silence. It's the hum of the refrigerator, the tick of the radiator, the soft drip of a tap left a fraction open. These small sounds stack until the room feels like the inside of something living, something breathing at a very slow rate.

You stand there in an old t-shirt, bare feet on cold tile, and for twenty minutes nothing happens. No phone. No thoughts you're trying to have. Just the kettle singing its metallic song, the grain of the countertop under your fingertips, the cold air biting the back of your neck.

And in those twenty minutes, something rearranges. You don't know what. But when the light shifts from that thin January line to a warm slant, the oatmeal is in a bowl, the tea in a cup, and the kitchen just looks like a kitchen. And you look like a person who has been allowed, for twenty minutes, to be no one in particular.
